entries.gloss: The dynasty that replaced the Umayyads, mobilising under the Prophet's Household's name without intending to install that Household in power.
A former governor 'Ali had removed, forced on him by his own camp as arbitrator.
Abbasid operator in Kufah who sent the identical secret offer to al-Sadiq and to 'Abd Allah al-Mahd; al-Sadiq burned the letter unread.
The place where Banu Hashim leaders gathered and Muhammad Nafs al-Zakiyyah was floated as a possible Mahdi.
“People of the House”: the Prophet's Household, whose Imams this book studies.
“Conventional reconciliation”: resolving apparent contradictions between reports or practices by attending to the circumstances each answered, separating a fixed essence from its changing expression.
The promised deliverer expected to establish universal justice; in Shi'ah belief, the twelfth Imam.
“The one who rises”: a title of the promised Mahdi, linked with establishing justice and restoring religious guidance.
A Shi'ah official inside Harun's government, encouraged to stay there and conceal his Shi'ism because his position let him protect believers.

The formal oath of loyalty owed to a ruler (Arabic: bay'ah). Yazid's demand for al-Husayn's personal allegiance was the trigger al-Husayn refused; al-Hassan's treaty explicitly excluded any such oath.
Mu'awiyah's adviser who proposed the Qur'ans-on-spears stratagem and outmanoeuvred Abu Musa in the arbitration.
The Prophet's clan, whose leaders gathered at Abwa'.
A man reformed by a single indirect question from Musa al-Kazim about whether a house belonged to a free man or a slave.
The religious duty to promote right and oppose wrong; invoked by al-Husayn, by the Kharijites, and by al-Sadiq when distinguishing a righteous uprising from a false Mahdi claim.
Ma'mun's minister, a possible initiator of the crown-princeship; al-Rida distrusted him and warned Ma'mun about him.
The Prophet, Fatimah and the twelve Imams, whose sayings and deeds the Shi'ah accept as authoritative guidance.
The pilgrimage to Mecca; on Hajj Zayn al-'Abidin chose anonymity so he could serve his fellow travellers.
The relative who explained the hidden-Imam arrangement by comparing it to al-Husayn's household after Karbala.
The Abbasid caliph who imprisoned Imam Musa al-Kazim for about four years.
The apparently one-sided ten-year truce the Prophet accepted with the Quraysh; it produced more conversions in two years than the previous two decades of conflict.
Mother of Imam al-'Askari, known as Jaddah (“grandmother”); her own learning made her a refuge for the community after his death.
The Kharijite who assassinated 'Ali; a survivor of Nahrawan.
Juristic preference: a jurist's discretionary judgment where no clear textual ruling exists.
The Battle of the Camel, one of the two wars (with Siffin) that followed the outcry over 'Uthman's killing.
Followers who maintained that Muhammad ibn Hanafiyyah had not died but was hidden at Mount Radwa.
“Those who went out”: the faction that broke from 'Ali after the Siffin arbitration, holding that a single major sin expels a person from Islam.
The eastern province where the Abbasid missionary network was strongest, and Ma'mun's power base.
The Iraqi city that sent al-Husayn eighteen thousand letters, yet was exhausted and unreliable in al-Hassan's time.
The Night of Power; the night the Kharijites chose to assassinate 'Ali, believing it would earn greater reward.
The Abbasid caliph who pressed Imam al-Rida, under threat of death, to accept the crown-princeship.
'Ali's commander who was about to win at Siffin when he was recalled under threat.
The city in Khorasan where Ma'mun's court sat and where al-Rida was brought and pressed to accept the crown-princeship.
Governor of Syria who opposed 'Ali and later ruled; exploited 'Uthman's death for political advantage.
A Medinan scholar who pledged allegiance to a mistaken Mahdi claimant — Mutahhari's cautionary case for investigating before concluding.
A son of 'Ali whom Mukhtar presented as the Mahdi; his followers (the Kaysanites) held he was hidden, not dead.
Led the earliest recorded political use of the Mahdi idea, presenting Muhammad ibn Hanafiyyah as the Promised Mahdi.
Muhammad ibn 'Abd Allah, presented as a possible Mahdi on the strength of his name and lineage; al-Sadiq rejected the claim while supporting a righteous cause.
The collection of Imam 'Ali's sermons, letters and sayings, cited in this book by sermon number.
The battle where 'Ali confronted the Kharijites: of about 12,000, roughly 8,000 repented and 4,000 died.
The concealment of the twelfth Imam from public view, during which his guidance is understood to continue.
Analogical reasoning: extending a known ruling to a new, similar case.
The stratagem at Siffin: with 'Ali's side near victory, Mu'awiyah's troops raised Qur'ans on their spear-points to force a halt.
A companion condemned by Musa al-Kazim for quietly hoping Harun would live long enough to pay a camel-rental debt.
The seat of government where al-Hadi and al-'Askari were forced to reside in the military quarter (al-'Askar).
The battle between 'Ali and Mu'awiyah that ended with Qur'ans raised on spears and an arbitration.
The “Six Authentic Books” — the six canonical Sunni hadith collections.
Concealing one's true belief or intention under pressure, to protect oneself or one's community from persecution.
The oneness of God; the first of the two aims of every prophetic mission, alongside justice among people.
The dynasty of Mu'awiyah and Yazid, whose collapse opened the political opportunity al-Sadiq declined.
Mutahhari's name for the promised future in which tyranny, discrimination, war and exploitation no longer dominate human society — realised in this world, not deferred to the next.
Holding office under an unjust ruler — ordinarily prohibited, but permissible, recommended or even obligatory when it genuinely serves believers and reduces oppression.
Obligatory almsgiving; one of the duties Mutahhari insists remain fully in force while awaiting the Mahdi.
